title: Choosing your five
hookLine: pick five practices from this camp that actually fit your life

cards: Eight weeks, and the toolbox is full. The long exhale, the double sigh, the box. The morning preview and the evening review.
Two columns, mine and not mine. Three good things. The view from a mile up, and memento mori.
Walking, the body scan, a bedtime. One act of service a week. The phone in a drawer.
The sunset. Nobody uses all of them, and trying to would turn peace into a to-do list. This last week of the camp is about making it yours.

teach.b: The Roman philosopher Seneca, in an early letter to his friend Lucilius, warns against a restless kind of reading: dipping into book after book, never staying with any. A person who is everywhere, he says, is nowhere.
Better to spend real time with a few and let them sink in. Practices work the same way. Five you actually do will change you more than twenty you admire.
So how do you choose? Three questions.
First, which ones did you enjoy? Not the ones you think you should like; the ones where something in you said yes.
Second, which fit your real life, not your ideal one? If mornings are chaos with small kids, the morning preview may need to wait, and the evening review may fit instead.
If you walk the dog anyway, walking meditation is already half done. Third, attach each practice to something you already do.
Psychologists call this an implementation intention: when this happens, I'll do that. When the kettle boils, three long exhales. When I lie down, the scan.
When the sun sets, the lamp. In Peter Gollwitzer's research, a plan in this form made people noticeably more likely to follow through. One last thing: these five aren't a prescription.
The practices came from Stoics, Buddhists, Jews, Christians, Sikhs, scientists, and a man in the woods in Concord.
The five you choose are yours, not mine.

how: People building a personal practice usually choose a handful of habits rather than many, and tie each one to an existing moment in the day, like waking, a meal, a walk or bedtime.

practice: Let the camp's practices drift by, one at a time, and notice which ones make you lean in. Pick five, and give each an anchor, said inside as a sentence: when I, then I. If you get stuck at three, that's fine; three is a start.
